options: 3 — each setter applies to the result of the previous one, like `count = count + 1`.
1 — all three calls read the same snapshot (0), compute 1, and queue the same replacement.
0 — React compares each queued value with the current state and bails out when they are equal.
1, but only because batching merges the three calls; without batching the count would reach 3.
mcqs.explanation: State inside a render is a snapshot: `count` is a `const` bound to 0 for the whole handler, so each line computes 0 + 1 and queues the replacement 1; the queue is applied in order, and only the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` composes against the pending value, which is what would produce 3 (https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot, https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates). The strongest distractor is option 0: it treats the setter as an assignment that mutates the captured variable, but `setCount` never writes to `count`. Option 3 is wrong for a different reason: batching changes how many renders the three updates cause (one, with the React 18 root), not the arithmetic — without batching the same code would re-render three times and still land on 1, because every call was built from 0. Option 2 invents an equality bailout: React does not compare queued values against the current state to drop updates.

mcqs.question: `<Counter />` is rendered three times in the same list. Each instance calls `useState`, then `useEffect`, then a custom `useOnlineStatus()` that itself calls `useState`. Which statement describes how React associates each call with its stored state?
options: By the Hook's function name, so every `useState` call in the tree shares one slot keyed by `useState`.
By the variable names in the destructuring, so renaming `count` to `total` resets that state.
Per instance, by the order of Hook calls in that render: the first `useState` of one instance and the first `useState` of another occupy different slots.
By component type, so all three `<Counter />` instances share one list of Hook state and update together.
mcqs.explanation: React keeps a positional list per component instance and walks it in call order; neither the Hook's name nor the variable name reaches that list, which is why a conditional Hook shifts every later slot and produces 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render' (https://react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks). The strongest distractor is option 3: state is per instance, not per type — three `<Counter />` elements own three independent lists, which is also why moving one elsewhere in the tree remounts it. Option 0 fails because `useState` has no global slot, and option 1 fails because renaming `count` changes nothing at runtime. A custom Hook does not get a separate list either: its `useState` is appended to the calling component's list at the position where the Hook is invoked (https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks).

mcqs.question: A list renders `items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)` and each Row keeps local state. The user types into row 0's input, then a new item is prepended to the front. What happens?
options: React throws a key warning and re-renders the whole list from scratch, losing all state
The new item appears first and the typed text stays with the item the user was editing
The typed text now appears in the new first row, because position 0's component state was reused for the new item
Nothing visible changes until reload, because keys only affect DOM reuse performance
mcqs.explanation: With index keys React matches children by position: the component instance and its DOM at position 0 are reused and receive the new item's props, so the typed state lands on the wrong data, and every row's state shifts (https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists). The strongest distractor is option 1: that is what stable id keys would do, since identity-based matching inserts a new node and keeps each row's state with its item. Option 3 is the classic 'keys are a perf hint' misconception; the failure is correctness, not speed, and index keys produce no warning.

mcqs.question: An Effect reads the `roomId` prop but is declared with `[]` dependencies. The prop later changes from 'general' to 'music'. What is the state of the subscription?
options: It resubscribes automatically, because React tracks which props the Effect reads
It stays connected to 'general', because the Effect's closure still holds the initial roomId
It reconnects on every render, because an empty dependency list means run after each commit
React throws a dependency-array error at runtime
mcqs.explanation: The dependency array is a description of the reactive values the Effect reads, compared with `Object.is`; `[]` declares 'no reactive values', so the setup from the first render, with roomId 'general', is never torn down or rerun, leaving the subscription stale while the UI shows the new room (https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect). The strongest distractor is option 2: it confuses `[]` with omitting the array entirely; omitting it runs after every commit, while `[]` never resynchronizes. The fix is `[roomId]` plus cleanup that disconnects the old room.

mcqs.question: In development with Strict Mode enabled, an Effect with cleanup runs which sequence after mount?
options: setup, then setup again, with cleanup only on unmount
setup, cleanup, setup
cleanup, setup, so the final state is one active setup
setup only, because Strict Mode does not change Effect execution
mcqs.explanation: Strict Mode in development remounts components after the initial mount to expose missing cleanup, producing setup, cleanup, setup; production does not perform the extra pass (https://react.dev/reference/react/StrictMode). The strongest distractor is option 0: the entire point of the remount is to run your cleanup between setups, so if the double setup breaks the app, the missing cleanup is the bug, not the development check.

options: It skips rendering: `memo` short-circuits the parent's render before the context is read.
It skips rendering: the provider compares `{ theme: 'dark' }` with the previous value structurally and treats it as equal.
It re-renders: a context update is delivered to readers directly, and `memo` only skips renders caused by equal props from the parent.
It re-renders, and so does every descendant of the provider, whether or not it reads the context, because a context change invalidates the whole subtree.
mcqs.explanation: `memo` compares the props a parent passes and has no say over a context read, so a consumer re-renders whenever the provider's value changes — the docs state that skipping with `memo` does not prevent children from receiving fresh context values (https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext). The strongest distractor is option 0: it treats `memo` as a shield around the whole subtree, but the context update path does not go through the props comparison at all. Option 1 swaps identity for structural equality: React compares provider values with `Object.is`, and the inline object is new on every `App` render, so even a value with identical fields counts as changed. Option 3 overstates the blast radius: descendants that do not read the context can still be skipped, which is why splitting contexts by change rate and stabilising the value with `useMemo` are the real levers.

mcqs.question: In a React 19 app, a parent renders `<SearchInput ref={inputRef} />`. The function component is declared as `function SearchInput({ ref, placeholder })` and passes `ref` to an `<input>`. What is correct?
options: React strips `ref` from the props before the component runs, so `inputRef` stays null unless the component is wrapped in `forwardRef`.
The ref arrives as a regular prop, reaches the `<input>`, and no `forwardRef` wrapper is required.
Only callback refs work as props; an object ref created with `useRef` still requires `forwardRef`.
It works only when the parent targets a DOM element; a ref to a custom function component must still go through `useImperativeHandle` to arrive at all.
mcqs.explanation: React 19 makes `ref` a regular prop for function components, so destructuring it and forwarding it to a DOM node works without `forwardRef`, which remains supported for existing code but is no longer required (https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19#ref-as-a-prop). The strongest distractor is option 0: it describes the pre-19 behaviour, where `ref` was extracted before props and `forwardRef` was the only way in — a reflex worth unlearning, not a current rule. Option 2 invents a difference between callback and object refs: both are values the parent attaches, and both now arrive as props. Option 3 confuses two separate concerns: `useImperativeHandle` narrows what a parent may call (for example `{ focus() }` instead of the whole node), it is not the mechanism that lets the ref through. The documented exception is class components, where `ref` still points at the instance.

options: It is invalid: like `useState`, `use` must run before any early return, or React cannot match the Hook's slot.
It is valid: `use` may be called conditionally during render, so non-admin renders never read the promise.
It is invalid: `use` can only be called from an async component that awaits the promise.
It is valid only in a Server Component; in a client component the promise must be read with `useEffect` and state.
mcqs.explanation: `use` is not a Hook: it does not claim a slot in a positional list, so it is legal inside `if` blocks and loops as long as it runs during render inside a component or a Hook (https://react.dev/reference/react/use). The strongest distractor is option 0: it applies the Rules of Hooks by analogy, which is exactly the mistake `use` was designed to avoid — reading context or a promise conditionally is allowed, while calling `use` from an event handler is not, because that runs outside render. Option 2 invents an async-component requirement: client components cannot `await` during render, which is precisely why `use` exists there. Option 3 reverses the direction: `use` is the client-side way to unwrap a promise; `await` belongs to Server Components. Two constraints still apply: `use` cannot be wrapped in `try/catch` (wrap the component in an Error Boundary), and the promise must be cached rather than created inline during render.

mcqs.question: Which error will an Error Boundary NOT catch?
options: An error thrown while rendering a descendant component
A rejected Promise read by a descendant via `use(promise)`
An error thrown inside a descendant's `onClick` handler
An error thrown while a descendant renders for the first time
mcqs.explanation: Error Boundaries catch errors thrown while rendering their descendants, including rejections surfaced by `use`, but not errors in event handlers, async code like timers, or errors in the boundary itself; those must be handled at their source with try/catch and error state (https://react.dev/reference/react/Component#catching-rendering-errors-with-an-error-boundary). The strongest distractor is option 1: it looks like an async rejection outside rendering, but `use` routes the rejection through React's render error path, so a boundary above it does catch it.

mcqs.question: During a React Compiler rollout, a component mutates a prop during render, violating the Rules of React. What does the compiler do with that component?
options: It fails the build until the component is rewritten, because Rules of React violations are compiler errors.
It skips optimizing the whole component and leaves its behaviour unchanged; the ESLint plugin is where the violation is reported.
It optimizes the component but leaves only the offending statement uncompiled, so the rest of the component still gets memoized.
It compiles the component, logs a development warning on every render, and relies on the warning to get the mutation fixed.
mcqs.explanation: The docs state that it "safely skips optimization rather than risk changing your app's behavior" when it cannot verify code against the Rules of React, so the component keeps working exactly as before, unoptimized (https://react.dev/learn/react-compiler/debugging). Option 0 is the strongest distractor: build-breaking compiler errors exist, but the docs call them rare precisely because bailouts are the default; a production rollout would be unusable otherwise. Option 2 describes a line-level bailout that does not exist — the unit is the component or Hook, and `use no memo` excludes that unit explicitly. Option 3 confuses the compiler with the lint rule: the ESLint plugin reports the violation during development, while the compiler silently leaves the unit uncompiled. The impurity itself is a pre-existing bug the compiler surfaces but does not fix (https://react.dev/learn/react-compiler/incremental-adoption).

mcqs.question: Two sibling components both call `useOnlineStatus()`, a custom Hook whose body holds `const [online, setOnline] = useState(true)` and subscribes to the browser's online/offline events. What do the two calls share?
options: One `online` value, because the Hook's state lives in the module that defines the Hook and is reused by every caller
One `online` value, but only while both components render under the same parent
The subscription logic only: each call gets its own state, its own Effect instance, and its own cleanup
One `online` value, because React keys Hook state by the Hook's name (`useOnlineStatus`) instead of by the calling component
mcqs.explanation: A custom Hook is just a function that calls other Hooks: React associates the `useState` slot with the calling component instance, so two callers get two independent values, two subscriptions, and two cleanups (https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks). The strongest distractor is option 0: the Hook function is defined once at module scope, which makes the state look shared, but module scope holds the function, not per-call state; sharing the value itself requires lifting it, using context, or another store. Option 1 invents a parent rule that does not exist, and option 3 reverses the identity rule: state is keyed by call order inside each calling component, not by the Hook's name.

mcqs.question: A component holds three independent values (`name`, `email`, `newsletter`), each set directly from its own input and never changed together. A teammate proposes `useReducer` "because it is the scalable choice". What is the correct assessment?
options: Adopt it: a component with more than one `useState` call should always consolidate them into a reducer

There is no clear win: a reducer pays off when related fields change through several interaction types and centralizing those transitions improves readability or testing; for independent values it adds indirection
Adopt it: dispatching bails out of re-rendering when the next state is deep-equal to the previous one, so the reducer is the performance choice
Reject it: `useReducer` only works with object state, so the three fields would have to be merged first
mcqs.explanation: `useReducer` moves the next-state calculation into one pure reducer and is worth it when actions describe related transitions that benefit from being centralized, read, and tested; plain independent values are exactly the case where `useState` stays simpler (https://react.dev/learn/extracting-state-logic-into-a-reducer, https://react.dev/reference/react/useReducer). The strongest distractor is option 2: it converts a code-organization choice into a performance claim, but the docs state that `useReducer` is not automatically faster, and React compares state with `Object.is`, not deep equality. Option 0 is a style rule with no support, and option 3 is false: a reducer can return a string or a boolean.

mcqs.question: A tooltip must be positioned from its measured height before the user can see it, otherwise the first frame flashes at the wrong offset. Which statement about the fix is correct?
options: Use `useLayoutEffect`: it runs after the DOM commit but before paint, so the measurement and the corrective re-render land in the same frame
Use `useEffect`: it runs after commit and before paint, so the node is measured before the browser shows anything
Use `useLayoutEffect`, which also runs during server rendering, so the first HTML already carries the measured offset
Use `useEffect` plus `setTimeout(0)`, because React 19 skips layout effects in function components
mcqs.explanation: `useLayoutEffect` fires after React mutates the DOM and before the browser paints, which is why it is reserved for measuring layout or applying a correction that would otherwise flicker; the extra render it can trigger still happens before the frame is shown (https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect). The strongest distractor is option 1: `useEffect` normally runs after paint, so the wrong offset can reach the screen first, which is the exact problem here. Option 2 is wrong in both halves: neither Hook runs during server rendering, and `useLayoutEffect` in server-rendered code warns and needs a client-only strategy.

mcqs.question: An async handler resumes after `await save()` and runs `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` with `count` equal to 0 in that render. The app uses React 18's `createRoot`. What is the result in the next render?
options: `count` is 2 after one re-render, because React batches the two calls and sums them
`count` is 1 after two re-renders, because updates after an `await` happen outside React's batching
`count` is 2 after two re-renders, because each setter commits before the next statement runs
`count` is 1 after one re-render, because both calls closed over the same snapshot; updater functions would be required to reach 2
mcqs.explanation: Automatic batching with the React 18 root API groups updates from promises, timeouts, and native handlers into one re-render, but it groups scheduling, not arithmetic: each `setCount(count + 1)` computes from the same render snapshot and queues the replacement 1, so the next render shows 1 (https://react.dev/blog/2022/03/29/react-v18#new-feature-automatic-batching, https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates). The strongest distractor is option 1: it keeps the pre-18 belief that async callbacks escape batching, so it predicts the right value for the wrong reason and doubles the render count. Option 0 confuses batching with updater semantics; option 2 treats setters as synchronous commits.

mcqs.question: A modal is rendered with `createPortal(..., document.body)` from inside a `<Layout>` component. A user clicks a button inside the modal. Which statement about the handlers is correct?
options: Only native listeners on `document.body` and above fire; the `<Layout>` React handler does not run, because the portal's DOM node is outside Layout
The `<Layout>` React handler fires as well, because React dispatches the event along the React tree even though the DOM node sits under `document.body`
No React handler above the portal fires: a portal opens a separate React root for events and context
The `<Layout>` handler fires only if the portal target is a DOM descendant of `<Layout>`; otherwise events stay contained in the portal
mcqs.explanation: A portal changes where the DOM node physically lives, not where it lives in the React tree, so context still reaches it and React events bubble through the React ancestors of the component that rendered the portal (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/createPortal). The strongest distractor is option 0: it applies the DOM ancestry rule and concludes the React parent cannot hear the click, which is precisely the misconception portals exist to separate. Option 2 turns a portal into a second root, and option 3 invents a containment rule that does not exist.

mcqs.question: A page re-renders on every keystroke in its search input, and eleven sibling panels that never read the query re-render with it. The Profiler shows the panels' props are identical between commits. What is the first fix to apply, before adding any memoization?
options: Wrap each panel in `React.memo`, since identical props are exactly what memo skips
Wrap the page's callbacks in `useCallback`, because new function props are what force the panels to render
Move the search state into the component that owns the input (or into a store read only by consumers), so a keystroke no longer re-renders the page
Read the search value from a ref inside the panels, so they render only when the filter actually changes something
mcqs.explanation: The documented order is to fix the data flow first: move state down to the component that owns the interaction, split the tree so unrelated work is not recreated, narrow the props, split a context that changes at the wrong scope, and only then reach for `memo`, `useMemo`, or `useCallback` (https://react.dev/reference/react/memo). The strongest distractor is option 0: it would stop the panels, but it leaves the page and every other descendant rendering, adds a comparison per panel, and does nothing for context readers; it is a second-line optimization, not the first fix. Option 1 does not remove a render caused by the page's own state, and option 3 means typing no longer schedules a render, so the filtered results would freeze.

options: Binding inside `render()` is the right fix: React creates a new instance on every render, so a bind in the constructor only protects the first one.
The real difference is speed: a function component never allocates the instance that owns `this`, and that is why the same handler written as a closure needs no bind.

`this` is decided by the call site, not by where the method is written: `onClick={this.toggle}` hands React the bare function, React calls it detached, and `this` is `undefined`. Binding once per instance in the constructor, or declaring `toggle = () => …` as a class field, gives the handler a receiver that survives the detached call.
The arrow field works because an arrow function has its own `this`, which React binds to the instance when it passes the handler; a prototype method never gets a `this` at all.
mcqs.explanation: The instance is created once per mount and reused across renders, so the only thing missing at the call site is the receiver: `onClick={this.toggle}` stores the function value, React invokes it as `handler(event)`, and a method called without a base object gets `this === undefined` because class bodies run in strict mode. `bind` returns a copy with the receiver fixed, stored once on the instance; the arrow field instead captures the `this` in scope when the field initializer runs, which is the instance created by `super(props)`. The strongest distractor is the speed one: if you only remember that function components never face this problem, it sounds like the answer, but it explains the class failure with speed, and the maintainers frame the historical gap as marginal — the choice is ergonomics and ecosystem, not performance. The actual mechanism has nothing to do with speed: a closure reads variables and no receiver is involved at all, so there is nothing to lose. The arrow-own-this distractor inverts arrow semantics, since an arrow has no `this` of its own and React never binds handlers. The bind-in-render distractor gets the instance lifetime wrong — one instance per mount, not per render — and rebinding in `render()` allocates a new function on every render, which defeats `PureComponent` and any `memo` comparison downstream (https://react.dev/reference/react/Component).

mcqs.question: You record one keystroke on a search page in React DevTools' Profiler. The commit detail shows `<UserList>` rendered although its props, state and context are identical to the previous commit, while `<Results>` legitimately re-renders because its `query` prop changed, and its expensive memoized rows skip. A `<Profiler id="results" onRender={…}>` around `<Results>` reports `actualDuration ≈ 4` and `baseDuration ≈ 38` for that same commit. Which reading is correct?
options: `actualDuration` is the time this commit spent in the profiled subtree with memoized descendants skipped, and `baseDuration` estimates that same subtree rendered from scratch, so the gap says memoization is paying off. Neither number says whether a render was avoidable; the commit detail does, which is why `<UserList>` rendering with identical inputs is the waste and the `<Results>` render is work you can only remove by changing the data flow.
`baseDuration` is how long the previous render took, so 4 against 38 means the keystroke before this one was the slow one and this commit is already back to normal.
`actualDuration` covers only the `<Profiler>` element itself, not its descendants, so the 4 ms is the cost of `<Results>` alone and the children's time is missing from the report.

Comparing the two numbers inside one commit means nothing: absolute render times are only comparable across devices, so the flamegraph width is the only usable signal and `baseDuration` should be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The docs define `actualDuration` as the milliseconds spent rendering the `<Profiler>` and its descendants for the current update, which is why a subtree whose `memo` boundaries skip shows up small, and `baseDuration` as an estimate of that whole subtree rendered without any optimizations, computed by summing each component's most recent render duration. The two are meant to be compared inside a commit, and a large gap is evidence that memoization is working — not evidence that the render was unnecessary (https://react.dev/reference/react/Profiler). Whether a render was avoidable is a separate question, answered by the commit detail: identical props, state and context mean the render could have been skipped, while a render whose input really changed is legitimate. The strongest distractor is the history one, because the pair reads like "now versus before": `baseDuration` is not history, it is a from-scratch estimate, and the before/after the docs recommend is the same `actualDuration` from two recordings of the same interaction on the same machine. The descendants distractor drops the descendants the parameter explicitly includes, and the incomparable one takes a real caution — absolute numbers do not travel between devices — and stretches it into "never compare these two", which is the comparison the API exists for. The workflow to narrate: record, interact once, read the flamegraph commit by commit, switch to Ranked to find the expensive component, open the commit to see which props, state or context changed, fix one thing and re-record the same interaction; and remember the instrumentation needs a profiling build in production, since profiling is off by default there.

scenarios.prompt: This search component works in local testing but intermittently shows results for the previous query in production. Identify every defect in the Effect, explain the exact sequence that produces the bug, and rewrite it correctly.
rubric: Identifies the race precisely: cleanup runs before the new setup, and with no cleanup an older response can resolve last and overwrite newer state.
Does not misdiagnose the dependency array: [query] is already correct; removing or adding deps is the wrong fix.
Rewrites with per-setup ownership: AbortController (or ignore flag) created in setup and torn down in cleanup, with AbortError filtered from error handling.
Distinguishes abort (cancels the request and its server work) from ignore (only discards the client-side result), and picks deliberately.
Names the production alternative: a framework loader or cache/query layer for deduplication, freshness, and cancellation.

scenarios.prompt: Step 1: the user types `call mom` into the note input of the row that shows `Buy milk`. Step 2: the user clicks "Add to top". After step 2, describe exactly what each of the three rows shows — the todo text and the note input value — explain the outcome at the reconciliation level, and give the minimal fix.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
After step 2 the list is: 'Wash dishes' with the note input still containing 'call mom'; 'Buy milk' with an empty note; 'Walk dog' with an empty note. The typed text ends up next to the wrong todo.

Why: with `key={index}`, React matches children by position among siblings. Position 0 previously held the 'Buy milk' `TodoRow` instance, whose local state contains note 'call mom'; after the prepend, position 0 receives the new item's props, so the existing instance is reused and re-rendered with 'Wash dishes' while keeping its state and DOM. Position 1's instance (previously 'Walk dog', empty note) is reused for 'Buy milk', and position 2 is a fresh mount for 'Walk dog'. The `todos` array and the props are correct; what is wrong is identity: React reused instances that belong to different items. No warning is logged, because index keys are valid keys.

Minimal fix: `key={todo.id}`. React then matches by identity, inserts a new node at the top, and each row's state stays with its item. Two related rules: keys are scoped to one parent's children, and the key is not passed to the component, so a row that needs its identity must receive `todo.id` as a normal prop. Source: https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists, https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state.
rubric: Predicts the exact end state: 'call mom' sits in the first row next to 'Wash dishes', not with 'Buy milk', and the other two notes are empty.
Explains position-based matching with index keys: the same position reuses the same component instance and DOM node while receiving new props.
Separates data (props, updated correctly) from identity and state (reused incorrectly), covering both React state and the DOM input value.
Gives the minimal fix, stable id keys, and explains why ids work: identity matching inserts a node without shifting every instance.
Knows the key scope rules: unique among siblings, not global, and not passed to the component as a prop.

scenarios.prompt: Refactor this comment form to React 19 Actions. Keep the same UX contract: the button shows a pending state, a failure shows an error message and keeps the typed comment, and the input clears only when the save succeeds. `saveComment` throws when the save fails. Explain what the framework now owns versus what you still own.
rubric: Wires `useActionState` correctly: the action takes `(previousState, formData)`, returns the next state, and the form uses the returned `formAction`.
Deletes the manual `saving` flag in favour of the hook's `pending`, explaining that a form action already runs inside a transition.
States that React resets uncontrolled fields when the action returns without throwing, that a returned error still triggers the reset, and preserves the failed draft through `defaultValue`.
Catches the expected `saveComment` failure into state, and can say when an unexpected error should be rethrown to an Error Boundary; keeps server-side validation authoritative.
Explains what is still owned (auth, validation, persistence) and optionally reaches for `useOptimistic` or `useFormStatus`.

scenarios.prompt: The cart starts empty and `fetchItems(['a', 'b', 'c'])` resolves with three items in that order. After one click on "Add three", predict the final `items` and `log`, state how many renders this batch causes, explain the mechanism, and fix the component so all three items appear.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Prediction: `items` ends as `['c']`, one element; `log` ends with three entries, `added a`, `added b`, `added c`; the batch causes one re-render, one commit.

Why `items` loses two updates: the handler closed over the render where `items` was `[]`. After `await`, that closure is still the same one, and `items` inside it is a `const` snapshot that never changes. Iteration a queues `setItems(['a'])`, iteration b queues `setItems(['b'])`, iteration c queues `setItems(['c'])` — three replacement values, not three operations against a pending list. React applies the queue in order for the next render, so the last replacement wins and the result is `['c']`.

Why `log` survives: `setLog` receives a function, so React runs each updater against the pending value while computing the next render: `[]` → `['added a']` → `['added a', 'added b']` → `['added a', 'added b', 'added c']`.

Why one render: with the React 18 root API, automatic batching groups all six updates — even outside an event, after an `await` — into a single re-render and commit. Batching changes the number of renders, not the snapshot rule: it does not make the replacements accumulate. On a legacy React 17 root the same code would commit six times, one per setter, and still end at `['c']`.

`flushSync` is not the fix. Forcing a synchronous commit between iterations would still run the rest of the `forEach` in the same stale closure, so every replacement would still be built from `[]` — it would only add blocking commits.

Fix with an updater:

`picked.forEach((item) => { setItems((prev) => [...prev, item]); setLog((entries) => [...entries, `added ${item.id}`]); });`

Or, since `picked` is already one batch, queue a single update: `setItems((prev) => [...prev, ...picked])`. Prefer the updater form over `setItems([...items, ...picked])`: the latter is correct for a single un-repeated click but breaks again if another add is queued before this render commits. Note that reading `items` on the line after the loop still shows the old value — verify the result in the next render, not in the handler.
rubric: Predicts `items` as `['c']` and `log` with all three entries, showing the two setters behave differently
Explains the stale closure: every iteration reads the `items` captured by the render that started the handler, so each call replaces with an array built from `[]`
Explains that batching collapses the six setters into one re-render without making dependent updates accumulate
Fixes with an updater (`setItems(prev => [...prev, item])`) or a single batched merge, and can explain why `flushSync` or re-reading `items` in the handler does not help
Notes that the result is verified in the next render, since the handler keeps the snapshot it started with

scenarios.prompt: The author added `memo` and `useMemo` to stop the chart and sidebar from re-rendering on every keystroke. `Sidebar` and `Chart` are memoized and receive no changing props. Predict what the user sees while typing, list which components re-render and which skip, name the defect, and give the smallest structural fix that keeps the filter label correct.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
What the user sees: the input updates normally and `HeavyTable` filters against the new query on every keystroke, but the `FilterOptions` line stays frozen at the initial empty query, so the label contradicts the results.

Which components render: `Dashboard` re-renders on every keystroke because it owns `query`; `HeavyTable` re-renders because it receives `query` and its output depends on it — that render is legitimate work, not waste; `Sidebar` and `Chart` skip, because they are memoized and their props are stable (`userId` does not change); `FilterOptions` also skips, which is the bug.

The defect is not `memo`: it is the cache in front of it. `useMemo(() => ({ pageSize: 20, query }), [])` declares that the object reads no reactive value, so the first object is returned forever. `memo` compares props with `Object.is`, sees the same object identity on every render, and skips — so the child never receives the new `query`. The dependency list is a description of what the computation reads, not a knob for "compute once" (https://react.dev/reference/react/useMemo). ESLint's exhaustive-deps would flag the missing `query`.

There is a second problem behind the first: once the dependency list is correct, `FilterOptions` changes on every keystroke, so `memo` can never skip it and only adds a comparison. The memo was compensating for state placement, which is the order the docs warn against: fix the data flow first, memoize only what measurement justifies (https://react.dev/reference/react/memo).

Smallest structural fix: extract a `ResultsPane` that owns `query` and renders the input, `FilterOptions`, and `HeavyTable`; `Dashboard` keeps `Sidebar` and `Chart` and renders `<ResultsPane rows={rows} />`. A keystroke now re-renders only `ResultsPane`: the expensive siblings are never even asked to render, and `FilterOptions` updates because it reads `query` in the same subtree. `memo` on `Sidebar` and `Chart` becomes a safety net rather than the mechanism, and can stay if it is already there.

Minimum patch if the extraction is out of scope: change the deps to `[query]` so correctness returns, and drop `memo` from `FilterOptions` unless the Profiler shows the comparison paying for itself. Do not wrap `Dashboard` in `memo` — its props are stable but its own state changes, which `memo` never blocks.
rubric: Predicts a stale filter label while the table results update, and identifies the empty dependency list as the cause
Explains that `memo` skips because the memoized object keeps the same identity, so the child never sees the new `query`
Separates legitimate renders (`Dashboard`, `HeavyTable`) from skipped ones (`Sidebar`, `Chart`, and wrongly `FilterOptions`)
Proposes moving the search state into a subtree that contains the input and its consumers, instead of memoizing around the problem
Frames `memo`/`useMemo` as second-line, measured fixes, and rejects wrapping `Dashboard` itself as a solution

scenarios.prompt:
An app shell drills `selected` and `onSelect` through `Toolbar` and `Sidebar`, and neither reads them. In React DevTools' Profiler, one keystroke in the toolbar search field renders `App`, `Toolbar`, `Sidebar`, `UserList` and `UserProfile`, and the commit detail shows `<UserProfile>` rendered with props identical to the previous commit. One row click renders `App`, `Toolbar`, `Sidebar` and `UserList`, and this time `<UserList>`'s props are identical. Every feature adds another prop to the wrapper signatures, and inserting a level between `Sidebar` and `UserList` means editing three components. `Toolbar` renders the search input bound to `filter` and lays out its children; `Sidebar` consumes none of its props and only forwards `users`, `filter`, `selected` and `onSelect` down.

(1) Which of those renders are legitimate and which are avoidable, and why? (2) Give the cheap structural fix with composition and `children`/slots while the state owner stays near, with the code. (3) When the consumers sit far apart, give the Context or compound-components version with the provider and a memoized `value`, and say what each piece buys. (4) What breaks if the `value` is not memoized, and when is Context the wrong tool?
rubric: Separates avoidable from legitimate renders using the commit detail, naming the keystroke case (UserProfile identical) and the selection case (UserList identical) without reaching for memo first.

Rewrites the shell so wrappers receive `children`/slots instead of `selected` and `onSelect`, and states the observable payoff: signatures stop growing, a new level touches the shell only, and the profile leaves the keystroke render path.
Produces a Context version with a single owner, a `useMemo`d value whose deps are the real inputs, and either a guard hook or an explicit decision about what consumers outside the provider see.

Explains the unmemoized value as an identity problem (new object per provider render, `Object.is`, memo cannot rescue a context read) and orders the mitigations: shrink the provider, split by change rate, then stabilise.

Says when Context is the wrong tool — one or two levels, a single consumer, navigable state in the URL, large frequently-changing data in a store with selectors — and keeps the verification step (re-record the same interaction).
